 "D58": {
  "body": [
   "FMVSS 138 (49 CFR 571.138) requires vehicles of 10,000 lb GVWR or less to light a low-pressure telltale within 20 minutes of any tire falling to 25 percent below the placard cold pressure or the Table 1 minimum (20 psi standard-load, 23 psi extra-load P-metric), whichever is higher; a direct system reads sensors inside the wheels, an indirect system compares wheel speeds through the ABS sensors because a low tire shrinks in diameter and turns faster.",
   "Lamp check: the telltale lights as a bulb check when the ignition is switched to On with the engine off; a system malfunction is shown by the same lamp flashing for 60 to 90 seconds after each start (Volvo says about 1 minute) and then staying on until the fault is fixed, and the sequence repeats every start.",
   "A steady lamp means at least one tire is significantly underinflated: all four are checked with a gauge, inflated to the placard and, on a Volvo Tire Monitor car, the system is recalibrated; a lamp that lights on cold mornings and goes out later means marginally low pressure. Because the lamp only comes on at roughly 25 percent low, TPMS is no substitute for a monthly gauge check.",
   "Volvo's status screen (MY CAR > Settings > Car settings > Tire monitoring) shows all wheels green when the system is working and pressures are at or above spec, one yellow wheel for one low tire, all yellow for two or more, and all gray while the system is unavailable, which can need several minutes above 20 mph (30 km/h) to clear.",
   "Relearn on Volvo's indirect Tire Monitor: engine off, inflate all tires to the placard, ignition mode II, MY CAR > Settings > Car settings > Tire monitoring, OK/MENU, Calibrate tire pressure, OK/MENU, then drive; calibration completes while driving, pauses if the car is parked and switched off, resumes on the next drive, gives no confirmation when finished but reports a failure, and must be redone every time wheels or pressures change.",
   "Direct TPMS on these Volvos transmits above about 20 mph; when a sensor is moved its seal, nut and valve core are replaced, the car sits 15 minutes with the ignition off after sensors are installed, a different tire dimension needs the system reconfigured by a technician, wheels without sensors trigger a message after 10 minutes above 20 mph, and a temporary spare has no sensor."
  ],
  "car": "A 2016 V60 can carry either system: the MY CAR menu shows 'Tire monitoring' for the indirect Tire Monitor (this car) or 'Tire pressure' for direct TPMS. With a 38 psi placard, 25 percent below is 28.5 psi; in its TPMS section Volvo also notes the systems use temperature-compensated values, so clearing a warning may take inflating about 3 to 4 psi above the cold spec.",
  "src": [
   [
    "49 CFR 571.138 -- Standard No. 138; Tire pressure monitoring systems.",
    "https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-V/part-571/subpart-B/section-571.138"
   ],
   [
    "Tire Safety Ratings and Awareness | TireWise | NHTSA",
    "https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/tires"
   ],
   [
    "V60 Owner's Manual MY16 (TP 20238, USA & Canada)",
    "https://ldgsvccassets.blob.core.windows.net/pdfs/610e4b1a5665ac4d99bd89bd1971f063df1c7284/V60_OwnersManual_MY16_en-US_TP20238.pdf"
   ],
   [
    "Tire Monitor - introduction",
    "https://www.volvocars.com/us/support/car/v60/2016/article/c43f9d2decd9952dc0a801513772c990"
   ],
   [
    "Tire Care Essentials | USTMA",
    "https://www.ustires.org/tire-care-safety/tire-care-essentials"
   ]
  ],
  "qs": [
   {
    "q": "A 2016 V60's tire pressure lamp flashes for about a minute after every start and then stays on. This most likely indicates:",
    "o": [
     "One tire is 25 percent below the placard pressure",
     "A fault in the tire pressure monitoring system itself",
     "The temporary spare is low",
     "The system is in the middle of a calibration drive"
    ],
    "a": 1,
    "why": "FMVSS 138 S4.4(c) and Volvo's manual both describe a malfunction as the low-pressure lamp flashing (60 to 90 seconds, about 1 minute per Volvo) and then staying lit, repeating at each start until repaired; a low tire gives a steady lamp.",
    "src": [
     "49 CFR 571.138 -- Standard No. 138; Tire pressure monitoring systems.",
     "https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-V/part-571/subpart-B/section-571.138"
    ]
   },
   {
    "q": "Technician A says that after correcting the pressures on a Volvo with the indirect Tire Monitor, the system is recalibrated from the MY CAR menu and finishes on its own while driving. Technician B says the indirect system measures pressure with sensors inside each wheel. Who is correct?",
    "o": [
     "Technician A only",
     "Technician B only",
     "Both A and B",
     "Neither A nor B"
    ],
    "a": 0,
    "why": "Volvo's manual says Tire Monitor works from the tires' rotational speed through the ABS sensors, not pressure sensors, and that calibration is started from MY CAR > Settings > Car settings > Tire monitoring and completes while driving.",
    "src": [
     "V60 Owner's Manual MY16 (TP 20238, USA & Canada)",
     "https://ldgsvccassets.blob.core.windows.net/pdfs/610e4b1a5665ac4d99bd89bd1971f063df1c7284/V60_OwnersManual_MY16_en-US_TP20238.pdf"
    ]
   }
  ]
 },
 "D59": {
  "body": [
   "A puncture is repairable only when it is in the tread area, no larger than 1/4 inch (6 mm) in diameter, and does not run into the shoulder or belt edge; shoulder and sidewall injuries are not repaired and the tire comes out of service.",
   "The tire is dismounted and inspected inside, including the inner liner; the repair fills the injury channel with a rubber stem or plug and seals the liner with a patch, often as a one-piece combination unit, and repairs may not overlap one another.",
   "Not acceptable: a plug alone, an outside-in repair, any repair made with the tire still on the wheel (Michelin calls an on-the-wheel plug-only repair unreliable and dangerous), and repairing a tire that already carries an improper repair, which is scrapped.",
   "A nail found in a tire is left in place and the car driven carefully to a shop, because a nail that has not fully penetrated may not have caused a puncture; a sidewall bulge is an internal failure and the tire is replaced immediately.",
   "Volvo's optional tire sealing kit is a temporary fix for tread holes only: the nail stays in, the tire is inflated to 22 to 44 psi within seven minutes (below 22 psi the hole is too large and the car is not driven), then driven about 2 miles (3 km) at no more than 50 mph (80 km/h) to spread the compound, kept under 120 miles (200 km) and 50 mph, and inspected by a technician who decides between permanent repair and replacement.",
   "Volvo warns the sealing compound can cause wrong readings or damage a direct TPMS sensor, and the empty compound bottle cannot be removed by the owner; a Volvo technician removes and disposes of it."
  ],
  "car": "If your V60 has the optional Volvo tire sealing kit, its 120-mile (200 km) and 50 mph (80 km/h) limits apply until a shop inspects the tire; Volvo says large holes or tears cannot be sealed and the hole must be in the tread, not the sidewall.",
  "src": [
   [
    "Tire Repair Basics | USTMA",
    "https://www.ustires.org/tire-care-safety/tire-repair-basics"
   ],

   ],
   [
    "V60 Owner's Manual MY16 (TP 20238, USA & Canada)",
    "https://ldgsvccassets.blob.core.windows.net/pdfs/610e4b1a5665ac4d99bd89bd1971f063df1c7284/V60_OwnersManual_MY16_en-US_TP20238.pdf"
   ]
  ],
  "qs": [
   {
    "q": "Which puncture is most likely repairable under USTMA's tire repair guidance?",
    "o": [
     "A 3/16-inch nail hole in the center of the tread",
     "A 1/4-inch cut in the sidewall",
     "A 3/8-inch hole in the tread",
     "A tread puncture that angles into the shoulder"
    ],
    "a": 0,
    "why": "USTMA limits repairs to the tread area, to injuries no larger than 1/4 inch (6 mm), and rules out anything extending into the shoulder or belt edge.",
    "src": [
     "Tire Repair Basics | USTMA",
     "https://www.ustires.org/tire-care-safety/tire-repair-basics"
    ]
   },
   {
    "q": "Technician A says a string plug pushed in from outside, with the tire left on the wheel, is an acceptable permanent repair for a small tread puncture. Technician B says the tire is dismounted, inspected inside, and repaired with a plug through the injury plus a patch on the inner liner. Who is correct?",
    "o": [
     "Technician A only",
     "Technician B only",
     "Both A and B",
     "Neither A nor B"
    ],
    "a": 1,
    "why": "USTMA rules out plug-only, outside-in and on-the-wheel repairs and requires dismounting, a full inner-liner inspection, and a stem or plug plus a patch.",
    "src": [
     "Tire Repair Basics | USTMA",
     "https://www.ustires.org/tire-care-safety/tire-repair-basics"
    ]
   }
  ]
 },
 "E1": {
  "body": [
   "Brake complaint diagnosis starts by placing the driver's report into one symptom: low or spongy pedal, high pedal effort, pulling, grabbing, dragging, noise or vibration.",
   "Bendix lists air in the hydraulic system, low master cylinder fluid and contaminated fluid among the causes of a low or spongy pedal, and worn or glazed pads, frozen calipers and booster failure among the causes of high pedal effort.",
   "A pull to one side under braking points to contaminated or mismatched pads, a seized caliper or a collapsed brake hose; dragging brakes can come from a blocked master cylinder bypass port or a sticking wheel cylinder.",
   "A high-pitched squeal or grind usually means worn pads, often the metal wear tab touching the rotor; pulsation through the pedal sends the technician to the rotors first, then to uneven pad wear.",
   "Volvo notes that a pedal that travels farther than normal and needs more foot pressure means a longer stopping distance, and a warning light comes on for the fault."
  ],
  "car": "Volvo's manual says the V60 has two separate hydraulic brake circuits, so the car can still stop on one if the other fails. Water from rain, slush or a car wash can delay braking until light pedal applications dry the discs and pads.",
  "src": [
   [
    "Brake Problems | Bendix Brakes",
    "https://www.bendix.com.au/faqs/brake-problems"
   ],
   [
    "Spotting Brake System Failures | Bendix Brakes",
    "https://www.bendix.com.au/news-events/spotting-brake-system-failures"
   ],
   [
    "Volvo 2016 V60 US Owner's Manual (TP20238)",
    "https://ldgsvccassets.blob.core.windows.net/pdfs/610e4b1a5665ac4d99bd89bd1971f063df1c7284/V60_OwnersManual_MY16_en-US_TP20238.pdf"
   ]
  ],
  "qs": [
   {
    "q": "A car pulls to one side only when the brakes are applied. Which is the most likely cause?",
    "o": [
     "Air in the hydraulic system",
     "A seized caliper",
     "Low fluid in the master cylinder",
     "A failed brake booster"
    ],
    "a": 1,
    "why": "Bendix lists a seized caliper and contaminated or mismatched pads as causes of brake pull. Air and low fluid give a low pedal, and booster failure gives high pedal effort.",
    "src": [
     "Brake Problems | Bendix Brakes",
     "https://www.bendix.com.au/faqs/brake-problems"
    ]
   },
   {
    "q": "A customer reports a spongy brake pedal. Technician A says air in the hydraulic system could cause it. Technician B says worn, glazed pads are the most likely cause. Who is correct?",
    "o": [
     "Technician A only",
     "Technician B only",
     "Both A and B",
     "Neither A nor B"
    ],
    "a": 0,
    "why": "Bendix links a low or spongy pedal to air in the system, low fluid or contaminated fluid. Worn or glazed pads are listed under high pedal effort, not a spongy pedal.",
    "src": [
     "Brake Problems | Bendix Brakes",
     "https://www.bendix.com.au/faqs/brake-problems"
    ]
   }
  ]
 },
 "E2": {
  "body": [
   "The master cylinder reservoir is checked for fluid level, fluid condition and signs of leakage at the reservoir, its cap and the master cylinder body.",
   "FMVSS 135 requires a separate reservoir compartment for each brake subsystem, so a leak from one compartment cannot drain the other, and the level must be checkable without opening the reservoir.",
   "The same standard requires a permanent label within 100 mm of the filler cap that begins 'WARNING: Clean filler cap before removing' and names the correct fluid type.",
   "Brembo says dark or cloudy fluid carries impurities and should be replaced; ATE recommends testing the fluid's boiling point and replacing it when the reading is below 180 °C.",
   "A low level can mean a leak, so the lines and fittings are inspected next; Cardone also says to check the master cylinder for leaking fluid before fitting a new brake booster."
  ],
  "car": "The V60's reservoir sits under a round cover at the rear of the engine compartment; Volvo says to check that the level is between MIN and MAX without removing the cap, and not to drive if it is below MIN. Volvo specifies DOT 4 fluid with a boiling point above 536 °F (280 °C).",
  "src": [
   [
    "49 CFR 571.135 -- Standard No. 135; Light vehicle brake systems.",
    "https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-V/part-571/subpart-B/section-571.135"
   ],

    "https://www.ate-brakes.com/media/2310/download_broschuere_bremsfluessigkeit_en.pdf"

   [
    "Volvo 2016 V60 US Owner's Manual (TP20238)",

   ]
  ],

   {
    "q": "On a 2016 V60, the brake fluid is below the MIN mark and a brake message is shown in the display. According to Volvo, what is the correct action?",

     "Do not drive; have the car towed and the brakes inspected",

    "why": "Volvo's manual says that if the level is below MIN or a brake message is shown, the car must not be driven and should be towed to a Volvo technician for inspection.",
    "src": [
     "Volvo 2016 V60 US Owner's Manual (TP20238)",
     "https://ldgsvccassets.blob.core.windows.net/pdfs/610e4b1a5665ac4d99bd89bd1971f063df1c7284/V60_OwnersManual_MY16_en-US_TP20238.pdf"
    ]
   },

    "src": [

   }

 "E3": {
  "body": [
   "Flexible hoses carry fluid from the fixed brake lines to the calipers; they must flex with the steering and suspension without swelling under pressure.",
   "Bendix lists cracks of any size, bubbles or bulges, leaks or stains, and corroded fittings as reasons to replace a hose; most vehicle makers set no replacement interval.",
   "Hoses are checked by eye and by feel, and a helper pumping the pedal shows whether a hose balloons under pressure.",
   "Lines and fittings are checked for leaks and damage; a collapsed hose can cause a pull to one side, and kinked or clogged lines and hoses can make the brakes grab.",
   "Under DOT rules and SAE J1401, a hose must hold 4,000 psi of water pressure for two minutes, and its end fitting must show no base-metal corrosion after 24 hours of salt spray."
  ],
  "car": null,
  "src": [
   [
    "Brake hoses are a small component with a big job says Bendix | Bendix Brakes",

   ],

     "No action; hoses are meant to expand under pressure"
    ],
    "a": 0,

    "src": [
     "Brake hoses are a small component with a big job says Bendix | Bendix Brakes",

 "E4": {
  "body": [
   "FMVSS 135 requires a brake warning indicator that lights for low fluid in any reservoir compartment, a gross loss of fluid pressure, an electrical failure in the ABS, or an applied parking brake.",
   "The lamps are tested at key-on: each indicator must light as a function check when the ignition is turned on with the engine off, and must stay lit for as long as its fault exists.",
   "The standard calls for red on the main brake warning and yellow on the ABS warning, labelled 'Brake' and 'ABS' (or 'Antilock'/'Anti-lock').",
   "Volvo says that when the ABS lamp lights, the normal brakes still work; the check is to stop, switch off, restart, and have the car inspected if the lamp stays on.",
   "The ABS circuits are fused; the 2016 V60 engine-compartment fuse box has ABS pump (40 A), ABS valves (20 A) and ABS (5 A) fuses."
  ],
  "car": "On the 2016 V60 all warning symbols light in ignition mode II or at start and should go out once the engine runs, except the parking brake symbol. If the red brake and yellow ABS symbols light together, Volvo says brake force distribution may be at fault.",
  "src": [
   [
    "49 CFR 571.135 -- Standard No. 135; Light vehicle brake systems.",
    "https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-V/part-571/subpart-B/section-571.135"
   ],
   [
    "Volvo 2016 V60 US Owner's Manual (TP20238)",
    "https://ldgsvccassets.blob.core.windows.net/pdfs/610e4b1a5665ac4d99bd89bd1971f063df1c7284/V60_OwnersManual_MY16_en-US_TP20238.pdf"
   ]
  ],
  "qs": [
   {

    "o": [
     "Fluid in a reservoir compartment below the safe level",
     "An electrical failure in the antilock system",
     "Application of the parking brake",
     "Worn pads on a vehicle with no electrical lining-wear warning"
    ],
    "a": 3,
    "why": "FMVSS 135 requires the indicator for low reservoir fluid, ABS electrical failure and parking brake application; lining wear is covered only where the maker uses an electrical wear warning device.",
    "src": [
     "49 CFR 571.135 -- Standard No. 135; Light vehicle brake systems.",
     "https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-V/part-571/subpart-B/section-571.135"
    ]
   },
   {
    "q": "On a 2016 V60, the red brake and yellow ABS symbols come on together. After a restart both stay lit, but the brake fluid level is normal. According to Volvo, what is correct?",
    "o": [
     "Do not drive; tow the car",

    ]

 "E5": {
  "body": [
   "The parking brake lamp tells the driver the parking brake is applied; FMVSS 135 requires the brake warning indicator to light whenever the parking brake is applied with the ignition on.",

   "The lamp test is to switch the ignition on, apply the parking brake and confirm the lamp lights, then release it and confirm the lamp goes out.",
   "FMVSS 135 also requires a friction parking brake that stays engaged by purely mechanical means.",
   "No sourced procedure for testing the switch or its wiring was found yet."

 "E6": {
  "body": [
   "Bleeding removes air from the hydraulic system; flushing replaces the old fluid with new fluid through the same bleeder valves.",
   "Bendix's procedure starts at the rear wheel farthest from the master cylinder: a hose goes on the bleeder valve, the valve is opened, and fluid is drawn through until the bubbles stop and clean, lighter fluid runs; the valve is then closed and the next wheel done.",
   "The reservoir level drops during the job and is topped up to the fill line between wheels.",
   "Pressure bleeders feed fluid in from the reservoir end; ATE's FB 5e offers 1.0 and 2.0 bar settings, which ATE says match leading carmakers' requirements, and uses a pulsing flow to help flush electronic brake systems.",
   "After all four wheels the pedal may have extra travel and the ABS lamp may light; Bendix says to pump the pedal until it is firm, cycle the ignition so the lamp goes out, then road test."
  ],
  "car": "Volvo's manual says brake fluid changes on the V60 should be done by a trained Volvo technician, lists the brake fluid volume as 0.63 US qts (0.6 liters), and says hard driving such as mountain use may call for more frequent changes. The change interval is in Volvo's Warranty and Service Records Information booklet and is unconfirmed here.",
  "src": [
   [
    "Bendix's tips for brake fluid change and bleeding using a brake bleeder kit | Bendix Brakes",
    "https://www.bendix.com.au/news-events/bendixs-tips-for-brake-fluid-change-and-bleeding-using-a-brake-bleeder-kit"

 "E7": {
  "body": [
   "FMVSS 116 sets minimum dry and wet boiling points: DOT 3 205 °C (401 °F) and 140 °C (284 °F); DOT 4 230 °C (446 °F) and 155 °C (311 °F); DOT 5 grade, which covers silicone DOT 5 and non-silicone DOT 5.1, 260 °C (500 °F) and 180 °C (356 °F).",
   "DOT 3, DOT 4 and DOT 5.1 are colorless to amber; silicone DOT 5 is purple; hydraulic system mineral oil is green and is not compatible with the rubber parts of brake systems built for DOT fluids.",
   "Glycol brake fluids are hygroscopic: they absorb water over time, the boiling point falls, and under hard braking vapor bubbles can form and the pedal can drop to the floor.",
   "Every container must warn to follow the vehicle maker's recommendations, keep the fluid clean and dry, store it only in its original tightly closed container, and never refill the container or use it for other liquids.",
   "Brembo warns that switching to a lower DOT grade than the vehicle maker specifies is dangerous, while moving from DOT 3 to DOT 4 is acceptable."
  ],
  "car": "Volvo specifies DOT 4 with a boiling point above 536 °F (280 °C) for the V60, well above the FMVSS 116 minimum of 230 °C (446 °F) for DOT 4, and says DOT 4 should never be mixed with any other type of brake fluid. Continental calls its ATE DOT 5.1 compatible with DOT 3 and DOT 4 but advises against mixing; for this car, Volvo's no-mixing rule applies.",

 "E8": {
  "body": [
   "This task covers removing a brake drum, cleaning off the brake dust safely, checking the drum for damage and measuring its inside diameter to decide whether it can be reused, machined or must be replaced.",
   "OSHA's guidance says to assume every brake shoe, old or replacement, may contain asbestos, because worn non-asbestos shoes cannot be reliably told apart from asbestos ones; exposure must stay below 0.1 fiber per cubic centimeter averaged over 8 hours.",
   "OSHA's brake appendix allows a sealed negative-pressure enclosure with a HEPA vacuum, or low-pressure wet cleaning that gently floods the assembly over a catch basin and lets the solution run between the drum and backing plate before the drum comes off; shops doing no more than 5 brake jobs a week may instead mist the parts with water and wipe them with a cloth. Dry brushing is prohibited in the wet methods.",
   "Brembo's shoe instructions say to work on one wheel at a time, keeping the other side as an assembly reference, and not to press the brake pedal once the drum is off.",
   "A 1944 SAE guide on drum reconditioning measures with an inside micrometer at the open and closed edges, at right angles to each other and at points in between, which reveals out-of-round, bell-mouth and bulge; it treated 0.010 in of out-of-round, or any bell-mouth, as needing reconditioning.",
   "Dexter's instructions say the maximum machining diameter is usually stamped on the drum, and to inspect the drum and resurface or replace it as needed. Pro-Cut's lathe manual says a drum that still shows excessive runout once correctly mounted should not go back into service."
  ],
  "car": "Volvo's press specification lists brake disc diameters for the front (300 to 371 mm, by rim size) and the rear (302 mm), and the owner's manual refers to brake discs and pads, so this car has no drum brakes to service.  "E9": {
  "body": [
   "Machining (turning) a drum on a brake lathe cuts a thin layer off the friction surface to remove scoring, out-of-round and other surface defects.",
   "Before cutting, check the drum's size and clean the mounting faces where the cones and clamps seat. Pro-Cut's lathe manual says the finished drum must never go past the vehicle maker's machine-to or maximum specification, because an over-machined drum is dangerous.",
   "When a spec book lists one figure as both the maximum machining and the discard diameter, Phoenix Systems says the trade stops 0.015 in short of it (a 9.040 in listing becomes 9.025 in), so the drum is not over the limit soon after it goes back in service.",
   "Pro-Cut's bench-lathe settings: cut no more than 0.015 in per side, always wrap the silencer band around the drum, and run small drums faster (180 RPM up to 12 in, 140 RPM for 12 to 14 in, 100 RPM for 14 to 19.5 in).",
   "Feed rate sets the finish. Pro-Cut cites about 100 micro-inch Ra as the upper roughness limit for many vehicles, reached at its coarsest feed with its own inserts, and about 45 micro-inch at its finest.",
   "Measure again after the cut and replace the drum if it is past the limit. Clean the friction surface before fitting, because machining leaves fine metal dust (Phoenix Systems)."
  ],
  "car": "Volvo's press specification lists brake disc diameters for the front (300 to 371 mm, by rim size) and the rear (302 mm), and the owner's manual refers to brake discs and pads, so this car has no drums to machine.",

 "E10": {
  "body": [
   "This task covers taking the shoes, return and hold-down springs, adjuster and other hardware off the backing plate, cleaning them and deciding what must be replaced.",
   "Work on one side at a time and keep the other side assembled as a reference (Brembo). Phoenix Systems lays the parts out in the order they came off, and Dexter's instructions say to note where the adjuster and springs sit before removal.",
   "Under OSHA's low-pressure wet method, the backing plate, shoes and shoe hardware are washed thoroughly before the old shoes come off; dry brushing is prohibited.",
   "Brembo says to replace any damaged brake part found during the job and any part contaminated with grease, oil or mineral-based cleaner, and to replace shoes on both wheels of an axle.",
   "Check the shoe lands, the raised pads on the backing plate the shoes slide on. Phoenix Systems says worn lands change where the shoe sits, and the backing plate must then be repaired or replaced.",
   "Dexter's kits use new hold-down nuts and washers, and its shoes are not interchangeable: the primary shoe, with the shorter lining, faces forward and the secondary shoe, with the longer lining, faces rearward."
  ],
  "car": "Volvo's press specification lists brake disc diameters for the front (300 to 371 mm, by rim size) and the rear (302 mm), and the owner's manual refers to brake discs and pads, so this car has no brake shoes or drum hardware.",

 "E11": {
  "body": [
   "Drum brakes need a thin film of high-temperature lubricant wherever metal slides on metal, so the shoes can move on the backing plate and the adjuster can turn.",
   "Brembo says to use high-temperature-resistant grease only on the parts of the backing plate that touch the shoes, and never on the friction material or the inside of the drum.",
   "Dexter's instructions list the shoe rest pads on the backing plate (six on its brakes), the adjuster threads, and the shoe web areas under the hold-down washers.",
   "Phoenix Systems cleans the shoe lands first, then puts a light film of moly lubricant on every metal-to-metal contact point.",
   "For the adjuster screw, Dexter says to clean the threads with a wire brush, apply a light coat of high-temperature anti-seize and screw it fully in before fitting.",
   "Keep lubricant and dirty hands off the linings: Phoenix Systems washes hands or covers the linings with masking tape during fitting, and Brembo says any part contaminated with grease must be replaced."
  ],

 "E12": {
  "body": [
   "The wheel cylinder sits at the top of the backing plate; pedal pressure pushes its pistons outward, which forces the shoes against the drum (Wagner).",
   "To check for leaks, pull back each dust boot, or pry press-on boots down from the push rod with a dull pick. Phoenix Systems says a light sheen on the bore and piston is normal; fluid pooled at the bottom of the bore, or dripping out when the boot is pulled back, means the cylinder is replaced, and replacing both sides is the accepted practice.",
   "Corrosion inside a wheel cylinder can let fluid leak, which lowers hydraulic pressure and gives a soft or low pedal (Wagner). Phoenix Systems adds that fluid under the boots by itself does not lower the pedal, because the cup seals leak only on release, so a low pedal needs its own diagnosis.",
   "To check operation, push each piston in a short way and compare the effort; a piston that will not move or needs much more force needs investigating. Pushing too far can damage the seal (Phoenix Systems).",
   "Hydraulic pressure must be zero before the drum comes off, and the pedal must not be pressed with the drum removed, or the pistons can be forced out (Dexter, Brembo). Brake fluid is corrosive, and a new cylinder means bleeding the brake circuit (Brembo)."
  ],
  "car": "Volvo's press specification lists brake disc diameters for the front (300 to 371 mm, by rim size) and the rear (302 mm), and the owner's manual refers to brake discs and pads, so this car has calipers rather than wheel cylinders.",

   "Brake fluid irritates skin and eyes and damages paint, so spills are wiped up at once and cleaned with water."

   "Raybestos and Pro-Cut aim for 0.002 in of runout or less as installed, and Pro-Cut names excess runout as the root cause of thickness variation and pedal pulsation.",

   "On an on-car lathe, the hub, rotor and adapter mating faces are cleaned, the adapter nuts are tightened evenly (no more than 20-25 ft-lb in Pro-Cut's PFM guide), and the lathe compensates for runout before it cuts.",
   "Pro-Cut's PFM guide gives a cut of .004 to .020 in per side, with .005 in per side at most on thin solid or drilled or slotted rotors, and a runout target under .002 in.",
   "After the cut, runout and thickness are rechecked before the adapter comes off, the rotor must still be above minimum thickness, and it is washed with warm soapy water and wiped until clean to remove metal grit.",

   "Engines whose intake manifold cannot make enough vacuum, such as direct-injection, turbocharged and variable-valve-timing engines, use a separate vacuum pump; MS Motorservice says these pumps produce about 0.7-0.9 bar of vacuum and are mostly vane pumps on the end of the camshaft.",
   "ATE's pressure gauge unit reads vacuum from 0 to -1.0 bar and can test the vacuum system, including the brake booster, for leaks and correct operation."

 "E34": {
  "body": [
   "Hydro-boost uses pressure from the power steering pump, not engine vacuum, to assist the brakes.",
   "Cardone's test: with the engine off, apply and release the pedal 5 to 10 times to empty the accumulator, then hold light pedal pressure and start the engine; the pedal should drop and then push back against the foot.",
   "Accumulator check: with the engine running, turn the steering lightly against its stop for 5 seconds, return to straight ahead and switch off; at least one power-assisted brake application should remain.",
   "Cardone lists a slipping belt, low pump pressure or a restriction for a hard pedal, contamination in the booster for a pedal that stays down, and a hydraulic brake fault for a long or no pedal.",
   "For leaks and contamination, damaged hydraulic lines and rubber hoses more than 4 years old are replaced; pedal kickback, grabbing or hissing while braking can come from contaminated fluid, which a flush through an in-line filter may clear."
  ],
  "car": "Volvo's manual describes the V60's power brakes as vacuum-assisted, so hydro-boost does not apply to this car.",

 "F1": {
  "body": [
   "The task is to make the airbag (SRS) system safe before work near its parts, then restore power and confirm the warning lamp runs its self-check.",
   "FMVSS 208 (S4.5.2) requires any occupant protection system that deploys in a crash to have a readiness indicator that monitors its own readiness and is clearly visible from the driver's seat.",
   "Volvo's SRS covers the seat belt pretensioners, front airbags, side (SIPS) airbags, the front passenger occupant weight sensor and the inflatable curtains, all monitored by the SRS control module.",
   "In ignition mode I or II the SRS light comes on and should go out after about 6 seconds if the module finds no fault; a light that stays on after the engine starts, or comes on while driving, means a fault has been detected. If the SRS symbol itself fails, the general warning symbol and a text message appear instead.",
   "Volvo's owner's manual gives no disarm procedure for owners and says all SRS work belongs to a trained Volvo technician. Its only instruction for cutting SRS power is for a flood-damaged car: ignition off for at least 10 minutes, then disconnect the battery, before towing."
  ],

 "F2": {
  "body": [
   "Voltage drop is the voltage lost across a wire, connection, switch or ground while current flows. By Ohm's law (V = I × R), 10 A through 0.5 Ω loses 5 V.",
   "Drop only shows with the circuit working, because a multimeter's own battery cannot push normal circuit current; the meter is connected across the section under test on DC volts or the mV range.",
   "Starter example (Fluke): disable ignition or fuel so the engine cannot start, put the red probe on the battery positive post and the black on the starter battery stud, crank 4 to 5 seconds and capture the reading with AutoHOLD or MIN/MAX; then measure from the battery negative post to the starter housing for the ground side.",
   "Fluke's guide for that test is about 0.3 V on the positive side and about 0.2 V or less on the ground side (0.2 to 0.5 V total); higher readings point to corrosion, loose terminals or damaged cables.",
   "Where the maker gives no values, Fluke's general maximums are 0.00 V across a connection, 0.20 V across a wire or cable, 0.30 V across a switch and 0.10 V at a ground; low-current computer circuits should stay under 0.10 V and need a 10-megohm meter.",
   "Fluke suggests testing engine and body grounds first. Delco Remy notes that 1 V of drop costs roughly 30 cranking rpm."
  ],
  "car": "Volvo describes the V60 as a 12-volt single-pole system in which the chassis and engine block carry current back to the battery and the battery negative is connected to the chassis, so body and engine grounds are part of every circuit tested.",
  "src": [
   [
    "How to Check Starter Circuit Voltage Drop with a Multimeter | Fluke",
    "https://www.fluke.com/en-us/learn/blog/digital-multimeters/how-to-check-starter-circuit-voltage-drop-with-a-multimeter"
   ],
   [
    "Diagnosing Voltage Drops: Electrical Automotive Troubleshooting | Fluke",
    "https://www.fluke.com/en-au/learn/blog/automotive/electrical-automotive-troubleshooting"
   ],
   [
    "Tech Tip: Checking Voltage Drops | Delco Remy",

   ],

   ]
  ],

 "F3": {
  "body": [
   "Current is measured either by opening the circuit and placing the meter in series, or with a clamp-on (inductive) ammeter around the wire. Delco Remy prefers the clamp because it does not disturb the circuit and cannot be damaged by misconnection.",
   "An in-line meter with an internal shunt is generally for 10 A or less and must not be overloaded. Fluke's drain test starts on the 10 A jack and moves to the mA jack once current falls below 400 mA.",
   "With a clamp meter on DC, select A dc, zero the display with the jaws closed and empty, then close the jaws around the conductor and center it on the alignment marks; Delco Remy adds that the jaw arrow points in the direction of current flow.",
   "Parasitic draw is read with everything off, doors closed and modules asleep (Fluke allows 10–45 minutes; Snap-on says most vehicles shut down within 10 minutes), the meter in series between the battery post and the removed cable, and no cranking while in current mode.",
   "Guide values differ: Snap-on uses under 50 mA, Fluke treats over 100 mA as suspect, and Denso says draws above 0.35 A should be investigated. The vehicle maker's specification overrides all three.",
   "To find the circuit, pull fuses one at a time or read the voltage drop across each fuse until the current falls. Snap-on notes a scan tool left on the DLC (pin 16 is always live) or a keyless key nearby can keep modules awake."
  ],
  "car": null,

   [

 "F4": {
  "body": [
   "Continuity and resistance are checked with power removed: disconnect the battery negative or isolate the circuit, since an ohmmeter on a live circuit can be damaged. A fuse taken out of the vehicle can be tested without disconnecting anything.",
   "Set the meter to Ω and the continuity beeper, red lead in V/Ω and black in COM, then touch the probes to each end of the path.",
   "A steady beep with about 0.0–0.2 Ω means good continuity. No beep with OL or a high reading means an open circuit, a break, corrosion or a bad connection. The beeper typically sounds below about 25–50 Ω.",
   "Ground continuity is checked from bare engine block or chassis metal to the component ground; no continuity points to a broken ground strap or corroded terminal. Wiggling the harness helps catch intermittent faults, and testing a known-good part first proves the meter.",
   "Diodes and transistors are checked on the meter's diode scale, not the ohms scale (Delco Remy).",
   "A meter's small internal battery cannot load a circuit, so a voltage drop test with the circuit operating finds restrictions more accurately than a resistance check (Fluke)."
  ],
  "car": "Volvo's manual checks a V60 fuse by pulling it and looking at the wire from the side, and says to replace it with one of the same color and amperage; a removed fuse can also be read on the Ω range without disconnecting the battery.",
  "src": [
   [
    "How to Perform Automotive Continuity Checks with a Multimeter | Fluke",
    "https://www.fluke.com/en-us/learn/blog/digital-multimeters/how-to-perform-automotive-continuity-checks-with-a-multimeter"
   ],
   [

 "F5": {
  "body": [
   "Testing starts with a visual check (correct size, type and CCA; no loose posts, cracks, bulges or leaks; clean, tight connections) and a state-of-charge reading. Odyssey wants an AGM battery at 12.6 V or more before a load or conductance test.",
   "Load test (½ CCA): enter the battery's CCA, apply half that current for 15 seconds and read terminal voltage. At 70°F or warmer it must stay at or above 9.6 V; the limit drops in the cold, for example 9.1 V at 30°F and 8.5 V at 0°F (Odyssey's table).",
   "Denso removes surface charge first (a 150 A load for 10–15 seconds after charging), replaces a battery that will not reach 12.6 V open-circuit, and runs the load test twice about 30 seconds apart.",
   "Conductance (electronic) testing sends a small AC signal through the battery and correlates the response with cranking amps. Midtronics says it takes under two minutes, does not stress the battery and works on AGM and EFB when the matching battery-type profile is selected.",
   "Tester decisions set the service: Good, Good–Recharge, Charge & Retest (replace if it repeats after a full charge), Replace Battery (retest out of the vehicle first, since a poor cable connection can cause it) or Bad Cell–Replace.",
   "Conductance alone checks cranking health; Midtronics adds longer profiling and charge-acceptance tests for reserve capacity, which matter on start/stop vehicles."
  ],
  "car": "Volvo specifies a 12 V AGM battery with 800 A CCA for start/stop engines, so a ½ CCA load test on a matching battery applies 400 A, and an electronic tester should be set to AGM.",

 "F6": {
  "body": [
   "Control modules hold data such as adaptive fuel values, diagnostic results, idle settings and audio presets. Interstate notes that losing it can bring rough idle, harsh shifting, warning lights from reinitialized checks and other faults after a battery change.",
   "A memory saver keeps the modules powered while the battery is out, commonly through the OBD II port; Snap-on notes DLC pin 16 is a constant battery feed.",
   "Connect the memory saver before disconnecting the negative cable, wrap the loose clamp so it cannot touch metal, and leave the vehicle's systems off while the battery is out so the backup is not drained.",
   "The memory saver must be disconnected during an actual parasitic-draw measurement (Fluke).",
   "Volvo: switch off, remove the remote key and wait at least 5 minutes before disconnecting the battery so the control modules can store their information.",
   "After a disconnect, Volvo's power-window auto function needs a reset: raise the switch front to close the window and hold one second, release briefly, then raise it again for one second."

 "F7": {
  "body": [
   "Inspection checks the size, type and CCA rating; loose posts; a cracked, bulging or leaking case; dirt and moisture on top; corroded terminals; frayed or stiff cables; and a hold-down that secures the battery without being overtightened (Denso, Odyssey).",
   "Only batteries with access caps are filled: use distilled or deionized water and never fill above the level mark. A sealed AGM (VRLA) battery never needs water, and opening it damages the battery and voids the warranty (Odyssey).",
   "Corrosion comes off with a wire brush on metal and a wet rag elsewhere, wearing rubber gloves; Odyssey warns against solvents and other chemicals on AGM cases, and Optima suggests one tablespoon of baking soda in a cup of hot water for flooded-battery terminals.",
   "Replacement: ignition off, disconnect the negative cable first and the positive second, inspect the cables, seat and clamp the new battery in the tray, connect positive first and negative last, and torque the terminals to spec.",
   "The new battery must match the original's cold-start capacity; Odyssey installs an AGM battery only at 12.65 V or more and charges it first if lower."
  ],
  "car": "Volvo requires an AGM battery with 800 A CCA on start/stop engines. Its steps add removing the front and rear covers, the vent hose and the clamp screw, and waiting 5 minutes after switching off before disconnecting; the manual's maintenance page also describes opening cell caps to add distilled water, which battery makers say a sealed AGM never needs.",

 "F8": {
  "body": [
   "Slow, low-amp charging limits heat. Interstate notes flooded batteries are stressed above about 10 A, while AGM batteries can take 30–50 A; charge time is roughly amp-hours divided by charger amps (70 Ah at 5 A is about 14 hours, at 20 A about 3.5 hours).",
   "AGM batteries need the charger's AGM (Absorbed) setting: above about 15 V an AGM can overheat and vent through its safety valve, and Odyssey says over 15.0 V causes irreversible damage. Optima advises against gel settings on its AGM batteries.",
   "Manual chargers keep pushing current until disconnected and must be watched with the ammeter, a voltmeter or a hydrometer; automatic chargers switch to a maintain (float) mode when the battery is full (Schumacher).",
   "Optima recommends charging its batteries at no more than 10 A and floating at 13.2–13.8 V with at most 1 A; Odyssey's float voltage is 13.6 V at 77°F.",
   "Charge in a ventilated area with eye protection and no jewelry; never charge a frozen battery (Clore), and Odyssey says not to charge above 104°F (40°C).",
   "Volvo's rules for the V60 override generic advice: never use a quick charger, only a traditional charger; never connect a charger to the battery negative terminal, only the chassis ground point; and disconnect the battery from the car when charging directly at its posts."
  ],
  "car": "The V60 manual forbids quick chargers and the battery negative post for charger connections. Start/stop cars use an AGM battery, so the charger should be on its AGM setting; AGM makers' high-current figures do not override Volvo's quick-charger ban.",

 "F9": {
  "body": [
   "Cables are checked for frayed strands, damaged insulation, corrosion and acid damage. A good cable bends freely; popping or crackling when it is flexed means internal corrosion and the cable should be replaced (Denso).",
   "Every connection in the path counts: battery clamps, frame and body grounds, and the connections at the starter, solenoid and alternator.",
   "Hold-downs must keep the battery secure without being overtightened; loose hold-downs, loose connections and case swelling are part of routine inspection (Odyssey).",
   "Flooded-battery corrosion is cleaned with a wire brush and baking soda solution (one tablespoon per cup of hot water, Optima). Odyssey says sealed AGM batteries should show little corrosion and are cleaned with a wire brush on metal and a wet rag elsewhere, without chemicals.",
   "A visual check cannot show resistance inside a cable or connector; Delco Remy calls voltage-drop testing the only sure check of the current path, and Fluke notes burnt or blistered body-ground insulation means starter current has overheated it.",
   "Cables are sized for the current they carry, and Odyssey suggests a heavier gauge for runs longer than six feet; terminals are torqued to the battery or vehicle maker's figure."
  ],
  "car": "On the V60 one screw holds the battery clamp, a ventilation hose runs from the battery to a body vent and must be refitted correctly, and the manual says to check that the cables are correctly connected and tightened. The rally bar (22 ft-lb) is fitted only on R-Design models.",

 "F10": {
  "body": [
   "Before jumping, confirm both systems are 12 V, wear eye protection, make sure two vehicles are not touching, and keep sparks and flames away, because batteries give off flammable, explosive hydrogen.",
   "With the ignition off, the positive (red) lead goes to the dead battery's positive terminal or the maker's remote starting point, and the negative (black) lead goes last to a heavy, non-moving engine or frame ground, never to fuel parts, moving parts or sheet-metal body panels.",
   "Clore calls the negative battery post an unsafe final connection because a spark there can ignite battery gases. Interstate's jump-pack guide still shows the negative post; Volvo forbids it on this car.",
   "With two vehicles, start the booster's engine first, then the disabled one. With a jump pack, Clore limits cranking to 6 seconds, then a 3-minute cool-down to protect the starter.",
   "After the engine starts, remove the negative (ground) clamp first, then the positive, keeping the clamps away from each other and from metal.",
   "A jump start does not fix the cause; the battery and charging system should be tested afterward (Interstate)."
  ],
  "car": "Volvo's V60 steps: ignition to mode 0, red cable to the booster's positive and then to the V60's positive post under its folding cover, black from the booster's negative to the ground point at the top of the right engine mount (outer screw), never the battery negative.  "F11": {
  "body": [
   "The starter current-draw test measures the amps the starter pulls while cranking, normally with an inductive clamp around the battery cable. Delco Remy zeroes the clamp first, keeps the jaws fully closed, and points the jaw arrow in the direction of current flow.",
   "The battery must be good and fully charged first, because starting-system results depend on it (Midtronics). Disable ignition or fuel so the engine cranks without starting, and crank only a few seconds (Fluke uses 4 to 5).",
   "Midtronics gives 150 to 400 A as a typical cranking draw, depending on the vehicle, engine size and temperature; the vehicle maker's specification is the figure to compare against.",
   "High draw with slow cranking points to a failing starter (worn brushes, damaged bearings or a failing armature) or to cold, thick oil, which Midtronics says can make the starter work two to three times harder.",
   "Resistance in the circuit lowers both voltage and current (Fluke), so slow cranking with low draw calls for voltage drop tests on the positive and ground cables.",
   "A weak battery and a failing starter show nearly the same symptoms (slow cranking, clicking, intermittent no-start), so both are tested before either is replaced."
  ],
  "car": null,
  "src": [
   [
    "Delco Remy Diagnostic Procedures Manual for Starters and Alternators",
    "https://www.delcoremy.com/getmedia/30ff0e99-7084-451b-8f2a-6745dd18a3b5/DelcoRemy_DiagnosticManual_Updated_Digital.pdf.aspx"
   ],
   [

    "https://www.midtronics.com/blog/battery-health-starter-motor-correlation/"
   ],
   [

    "https://www.midtronics.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/MDX-650-EN-Instruction-Manual.pdf"

   ],
   [
    "Diagnosing Voltage Drops: Electrical Automotive Troubleshooting | Fluke",

   ]
  ],

 "F12": {
  "body": [
   "The starter control circuit is the low-current path that tells the starter to engage: from the battery through the start switch and any relay or magnetic switch to the solenoid's S terminal, and back to the battery.",
   "Delco Remy notes that too much voltage loss in this circuit can make the solenoid pull in and drop out repeatedly (chatter) or not engage at all, which also damages the solenoid's contact disc and terminals; a deeply discharged battery can cause the same symptom.",
   "In Delco Remy's solenoid circuit test, a carbon pile loads the switch lead to 100 A and a voltmeter reads from the solenoid BAT terminal to that lead; on a 12-volt system the loss must not exceed 1.0 V, and the wiring alone must not exceed 0.8 V.",
   "High loss points to loose or corroded terminals, wire that is too small, a switch mounted too far from the starter, or a worn switch, and those parts are repaired or replaced.",
   "Hella lists a starter that keeps running after the key or button is released as a faulty ignition switch or relay; the engine must be shut off at once and the switch and relay checked.",
   "For any cranking voltage-drop test, Fluke advises disabling ignition or fuel so the engine cannot start, setting park or neutral with the parking brake on, and keeping hands and leads away from moving parts."
  ],
  "car": "On the 2016 V60 with Start/Stop, the 30 A starter motor relay is in the engine compartment cold-zone fuse box, where Volvo says positions A1, A2 and 1–11 are relays or circuit breakers for a trained Volvo technician only. Pressing START/STOP ENGINE runs the starter until the engine starts, for at most 10 seconds per try.",

   [

    "https://www.delcoremy.com/getmedia/30ff0e99-7084-451b-8f2a-6745dd18a3b5/DelcoRemy_DiagnosticManual_Updated_Digital.pdf.aspx"
   ],

 "F13": {
  "body": [
   "Delco Remy checks the battery, cables and switch circuits before blaming the starter; if all of them pass and the engine still cranks poorly, the fault is the starter or the engine, and if a new starter does not fix it, the engine has a mechanical problem.",
   "Denso's removal order: disconnect the negative battery cable first, label each wire, disconnect the battery cable and the control wire at the solenoid, loosen the mounting bolts, then support the starter while removing them and note each bolt's size and location.",
   "With the starter out, inspect every tooth of the flywheel or flex plate, through the starter opening if there is no inspection cover; Delco Remy replaces the starter for a damaged pinion, and replaces the ring gear for a damaged ring gear while expecting the pinion to be damaged too.",
   "Compare the new starter with the old one: case, nose cone, mounting offsets and hole locations, connector positions and nose cone clocking (Denso). Dixie adds cleaning oil and corrosion off the mounting surface and moving heat shields, locating pins and alignment sleeves to the new unit.",
   "Torque the mounting bolts and terminal nuts to the vehicle maker's specifications, route the harness clear of other parts, reconnect the negative cable last, then start the engine several times, including once it is hot."
  ],
  "car": "Volvo's 2016 V60 manual warns never to disconnect the battery while the engine is running or the key is in the ignition, and after three failed start attempts to wait about 3 minutes so the battery can recover. The manual has no starter removal procedure, so the V60's bolt torques are unconfirmed here.",

 "F14": {
  "body": [
   "Test the battery first: Denso wants it fully charged (12.6 V) with clean cables, terminals and grounds, and Delco Remy wants it load tested and above 12.4 V with no load before the alternator is judged.",
   "Denso's output check: at about 2,000 rpm, voltage at the alternator and at the battery should be 13–15 V, then the test is repeated with headlights, blower and defrosters on; refer to the vehicle maker's specification.",
   "Delco Remy's current test loads the system with a carbon pile until an inductive ammeter on the output wire reads its highest value; output must be within 10% of the rating stamped on the alternator, and an output over 15.5 V means the alternator (internal regulator) is replaced.",
   "Wiring is checked by voltage drop: Denso allows 0.2 V or less on the positive side (output stud to battery +) and on the negative side (alternator case to battery −) at 2,000 rpm with loads on.",
   "Undercharge shows as slow cranking, low voltmeter readings and dim lights or slow turn signals; overcharge as high readings, a bad-smelling or acid-spewing battery and bright or burned-out bulbs (Delco Remy). For no charge, Denso lists a loose or worn belt, bad battery connections, a blown fuse or fusible link, wiring faults, a failed alternator or too much electrical load."
  ],

 "F15": {
  "body": [
   "Gates says modern EPDM belts rarely crack, so the old rule of three cracks in three inches does not apply; wear shows as rib material loss, and as little as 5% loss can cause problems.",
   "Worn ribs let the belt bottom out in the pulley grooves, causing slip and, when wet, hydroplaning. Gates' belt wear gauge is pressed into the grooves: if it rocks side to side, the belt is worn out; Gates suggests starting belt checks at 60,000 miles.",
   "Automatic tensioners are wear items. With the engine off and cold, swing the arm through its full travel: sticking or roughness means replacement. Side-to-side arm play means a worn pivot bushing (belt tracking problems), and a bouncing or chattering arm while running means a worn damper and a failed tensioner.",
   "Squeal points to low tension; Gates says to confirm the belt is the correct length before replacing the tensioner, and to spin each pulley to check its bearing.",
   "Denso: a belt that is too loose slips and charges irregularly or not at all, while a belt that is too tight damages the alternator bearings.",
   "An overrunning (decoupler) alternator pulley passes drive in one direction only, which cuts belt vibration and wear (Hella); Dixie warns these clutch pulleys have a short life and should be checked whenever an alternator is replaced."
  ],
  "car": "Hella's start-stop service example, shown on a Volvo V60, notes that start-stop systems use alternators with an overrunning pulley; whether the 2016 V60 T5 Drive-E alternator has one is unconfirmed. The owner's manual has no drive belt inspection or replacement interval.",

  "body": [
   "Confirm the alternator is at fault first: Dixie calls for a charged, load-tested battery, a voltage-drop test of the cables under load (over 0.2 V needs attention), a check of fusible links, and an inspection of the belt and decoupler pulley.",
   "Disconnect the battery before removal; Hella warns never to disconnect, short or connect battery terminals while the engine runs, because the voltage spikes can do damage. Denso then labels each wire, releases belt tension (an automatic tensioner is rotated with the proper tool), and supports the alternator while removing its bolts, noting bracket orientation and bolt lengths.",
   "Compare the new unit with the old: pulley offset, size, type and groove count, mounting holes, and connector locations or rear housing clocking (Denso, Dixie).",
   "Fit the bolts, install the belt, set tension and torque to the vehicle maker's specifications, check pulley alignment and harness clearance, and never pry or hammer on the alternator housing (Denso).",
   "Charge a deeply discharged battery before start-up rather than using the new alternator to do it (Dixie). Denso runs the engine 10 minutes to seat a new belt, rechecks tension to the used specification, and retests the charging system."

 "F21": {
  "body": [
   "Hella's diagnosis order: check for voltage at the horn connector, then the ground, then the horn itself. With voltage present, a horn that is silent or only hums usually has a torn or blocked diaphragm and is replaced.",
   "Check the fuse first; hairline cracks can be invisible, so Hella confirms the fuse with a multimeter and cleans corroded fuse contacts.",
   "With no voltage at the horn, check the harness for continuity; breaks are common where the wire flexes, near connectors and where it passes from the body into the engine bay.",
   "A weak, distorted or irregular sound usually means a poor ground or oxidized connectors. A jumper wire to ground isolates a bad ground point, which is then cleaned and protected with contact grease.",
   "If voltage and ground are good but the button does nothing, test the horn switch or steering wheel slip ring with a multimeter; disconnect the battery first and follow airbag safety rules.",
   "A replacement horn is mounted facing forward, sheltered from splash water, and clear of body parts so it can vibrate. Hella's example: a 66 W pair of horns draws about 11 A at 12 V, so the wiring, relay and fuse must suit the load."
  ],
  "car": "On the 2016 V60, the horn sounds when the steering wheel hub is pressed, and the horn fuse is 15 A in the engine compartment fuse box.",

 "F22": {
  "body": [
   "A wiper system is a DC motor, usually under the hood near the firewall, driving a linkage that turns rotation into a sweep, plus spring-loaded arms whose down-force is matched to the blade and glass (Trico).",
   "Trico lists louder motor noise, slower wiping, intermittent operation and wipers stalling mid-glass as signs of motor failure. An arm that stops or moves intermittently may have a loose pivot nut, which is tightened to the specified torque.",
   "Replace blades when they streak (torn, bent or sun-dried rubber), squeak (grime, dry glass, or worn rubber letting the frame touch the glass) or chatter (heat or cold set); Trico's general rule is every six months.",
   "To fit blades, use the maker's sizes (too long can scratch the glass), protect the windshield in case the arm snaps back, remove the rubber's plastic protector, click the blade in untwisted, then test at every speed with washer fluid; never run wipers dry.",
   "Hella lists washer faults as a bad power supply or connection, a jammed motor, a pump cracked by impact or frost, damaged or clogged hoses, a dirty tank, unsuitable cleaning agents, a leaking pump-to-tank seal, and a clogged or faulty nozzle or non-return valve. Dual-outlet pumps reverse direction to feed the front or rear."

 "G1": {
  "body": [
   "HELLA's A/C check is a visual inspection of every part plus a function and performance test: the high- and low-side pressures are read on gauges and compared with the maker's values, and the air temperature at the center vent is compared with the maker's figure.",
   "Cabin temperature comes from blending cold and hot air; on Volvo's ECC the driver picks where the air goes with three buttons (floor, dashboard vents, defroster), or AUTO, which runs temperature, A/C, blower speed, recirculation and air distribution by itself.",
   "In HELLA's pressure table, both sides high with vent air near outside temperature points to a dirty condenser, a condenser fan that is dead or spinning the wrong way, an overfilled system or an overheated engine; both sides low with warm air points to low refrigerant; equal pressures with ambient-temperature air point to no refrigerant, a failed compressor or an electrical fault.",
   "Many newer compressors have no clutch: they turn whenever the engine runs, and the climate control unit sets their output through a control valve fed a pulse-width signal, so a working compressor is confirmed by a change in signal followed by a change in pressure and vent temperature.",
   "Volvo's A/C pressure check (an attachment to TJ 34648) runs the engine with both sides set to 20 °C in automatic mode, all doors, windows and the tailgate closed, lets the system settle, then reads the gauges against Volvo's specification.",
   "Some behavior is normal on this car: Volvo says the A/C cuts out briefly at full acceleration or when towing uphill, switching the blower fully off also switches the A/C off, and the radiator cooling fan may run for up to 6 minutes after the engine is turned off."
  ],
  "car": "Volvo's fuse list gives 4-cylinder engines an \"A/C solenoid\" fuse (7.5 A, shared with fuel leakage detection) and marks the separate \"A/C compressor\" fuse as not for 4-cylinder engines; whether the B4204T11's compressor has a clutch is unconfirmed. Volvo's pressure-check attachment to TJ 34648 lists 2017-2018 V60s of this generation, not the 2016 model year.",

 "G2": {
  "body": [
   "Anyone who services a vehicle A/C system for pay or barter must be certified under Clean Air Act section 609 by an EPA-approved program (ASE is one), whatever the refrigerant, and must use refrigerant handling equipment certified by EPA, UL or Intertek (formerly ETL).",
   "Refrigerant must be recovered with that equipment before the system is opened, and recycled on site or reclaimed off site to AHRI Standard 700 before it goes back into any car, even the one it came from; venting is illegal for every MVAC refrigerant except CO2 (R-744).",
   "The refrigerant is identified by its service fittings: each EPA-approved refrigerant has its own set (R-134a quick-connect ports; R-1234yf quick-connects with 17 mm high-side and 14 mm low-side outside diameters), adapters may not be used to convert them, and EPA's assigned label color for HFC-134a is sky blue.",
   "EPA lists separate certified recover/recycle/recharge machines for HFC-134a (SAE J2788) and HFO-1234yf (SAE J2843); Robinair's R-134a unit is to be used with R-134a only, because mixed refrigerants damage both the machine and the car.",
   "In Robinair's sequence the machine recovers to 0 psi, drains the oil it pulled out (that amount of new oil goes back in), evacuates to remove air and boil off moisture, then charges the weight entered; Robinair's manual gives both a 10-minute minimum and a 15-minute recommendation for vacuum, HELLA suggests about 30 minutes, and the vehicle maker's figure overrides both.",
   "Since model year 2025, new light-duty vehicles cannot use refrigerants with a global warming potential of 150 or more, such as HFC-134a (GWP 1,430), but existing HFC-134a cars may still be serviced with HFC-134a."
  ],

 "G3": {
  "body": [
   "Leaks are one of the most common causes of A/C trouble: the charge drops unnoticed until cooling fades or fails, and a low charge also damages parts.",
   "HELLA notes R-134a slowly passes through rubber hoses and joints, with losses of up to 10% a year even in a new system, so a careful leak search is needed to tell a real leak from normal loss.",
   "With fluorescent dye, the dye is added to the system, allowed to circulate, and the parts are then scanned with a UV lamp; Spectroline says this takes 5 to 45 minutes depending on system size and works best in a dark area.",
   "An electronic leak detector senses halogen gas and sounds a tone, and can find very small leaks in places that are hard to reach, such as the evaporator.",
   "An empty system can be pressure tested with nitrogen (HELLA's maximum is 12 bar) and watched for 5 to 10 minutes for a pressure drop, with foam spray to show the spot, or filled with forming gas (95% nitrogen, 5% hydrogen) and checked by moving the sensor slowly above suspect joints, because hydrogen rises.",
   "Robinair warns never to pressure test or leak test an A/C system with compressed air, because some air and refrigerant mixtures can ignite at high pressure; HELLA lists leaks at the compressor shaft or housing among compressor failures."
  ],
  "car": "Volvo's manual lists the system as R134a with PAG oil and says climate system work needs special tools and a trained and qualified Volvo technician.",

 "G4": {
  "body": [
   "The condenser sits at the front of the car to catch airflow; hot, high-pressure gas from the compressor gives up its heat there and turns into a high-pressure liquid, helped by a fan or by air from driving.",
   "Because it faces the road, the condenser collects dirt and corrosion, and its coils can be bent, cracked or crushed by debris or impact; any of these cuts its ability to shed heat, and severe corrosion can cause leaks or blockages that call for replacement.",
   "Restricted condenser airflow shows on the gauges as high pressure on both sides with vent air that gets warmer, up to outside temperature; a condenser fan that is dead or turning the wrong way gives the same pattern.",
   "HELLA lists a high-side reading that drops when the condenser is cooled with water among the signs of this fault, and the fix is to clean or replace the condenser and check the fan."
  ],
  "car": "Volvo's manual advises removing auxiliary lights from in front of the grille when driving in hot weather, as part of avoiding engine overheating.  "G5": {
  "body": [
   "The cabin air filter cleans the outside air coming in through the ventilation system, trapping dust and pollen; some types also use carbon to cut odors and gases.",
   "A clogged filter shows as weak airflow on the highest blower setting, bad or musty smells from the vents, slower heating and cooling, and fog that is slow to clear from the windshield.",
   "FRAM suggests changing it at least once a year or as the carmaker recommends, and sooner in dusty or polluted areas or when the symptoms appear; HELLA includes a new cabin filter in its yearly A/C check.",
   "When fitting the new filter, keep debris from dropping into the blower motor; a blower that is louder after the change can mean something fell in."

  "car": "Volvo's manual says the cabin filter cannot be cleaned and must be replaced, more often in dirty and dusty driving, and that several filter types exist, so the correct one must be fitted; for the interval it points to the Warranty and Service Records booklet or a Volvo technician.  "G6": {
  "body": [
   "The A/C compressor is driven by the engine through a ribbed (serpentine) belt, so belt slip shows up as poor A/C performance along with weaker engine cooling and other symptoms.",
   "Gates says the old rule of replacing a belt with three cracks in three inches suits neoprene belts but not modern EPDM belts, which can pass 100,000 miles without visible cracks; on EPDM the wear is lost rib material.",
   "Worn ribs round off and the belt sits deeper in the pulley, so it grips less, slips, and can hydroplane on water; Gates says as little as 5% rib loss can cause trouble and suggests starting checks at 60,000 miles.",
   "With the engine off, a belt wear gauge is pressed into the grooves: if it stays seated and will not rock, the belt has life left; if it rocks side to side, the belt is worn out.",
   "Other reasons to replace: chunks missing (the belt can fail at any time), a rib separating from the base, or oil contamination (fix the leak first and do not use belt dressing); tension is checked with a tension tester on a correctly aligned drive.",
   "HELLA lists defective tensioning parts among the causes of compressor failure, and Gates advises checking the belt and tensioner together when any part of the drive gives trouble."
  ],
  "car": "Volvo's manual lists checking the condition of the drive belts before any long trip. It gives no belt tension figure or adjustment procedure, and whether this engine uses an automatic tensioner is unconfirmed.",

   "A drain hose that is blocked, kinked, loose or badly fitted sends the water into the cabin instead, with a damp front footwell carpet and a musty smell as the usual complaints.",
   "MINI's bulletin names three causes: a drain blocked by a heat shield, a drain not attached properly to the HVAC housing, or one damaged at installation; the drain is replaced if it is damaged or drains slowly, and if no leak is found there the water entry is searched for elsewhere.",
   "GM's fix for water on the front passenger floor is to dry the carpet and fully seat or reinstall the evaporator drain hose.",
   "Volvo recalled 2016-2017 XC90 and 2017 S90 models (R89707) because a misinstalled drain hose could leak condensation into the cabin, which over time could affect airbag and engine management electronics; the fix was to inspect or replace the hose and check any wet wiring under the carpet."

### `src/js/data/manual.js`

/* The workshop manual: the car is the menu.
   views  = places you look (hood open, the wheel, inside, underneath, walk-around). Each is a figure with numbered points.
   items  = the parts you can tap in a view. Each item is a small manual of chapters in order of difficulty:
            K Know it, C Check it, S Service it, D Diagnose it, U Upgrade it. Items only have the chapters there is sourced content for.
   steps  = things done in the rest of the app. Each step names the evidence that closes it:
            mission (Training), kb (Library article read), diy (DIY job done), tree (troubleshooter walked), tab (page opened),
            photo (a photo of that kind saved), record (a service record for that item), oil (oil checks logged), scans (real health checks),
            receipts, build (build month entered), tsb (bulletin marked), upg (upgrade decided), recall (recalls set), manual (the owner confirms).
   Order:   chapters open strictly in the order of the path (data/path.js), one step at a time (Kyle, 2026-10-15).
            CASE_OPENS no longer opens anything; it only labels which story case points at a part.
   Numbering is the manual's: view 1 is the engine bay, 1.3 the battery, 1.3.1 its first chapter.
   Positions (at) are on the schematic figures in manual.js, 358 wide. The owner's own photo replaces the figure once pinned. */
window.V60_MANUAL_DATA = (function () {
  var V = [
    { id: "bay", num: 1, n: "Engine bay", enter: "Open the hood", d: "Everything under the hood you can check without tools, and the parts you should only look at.", fig: "bay", hint: "Stand at the front bumper with the hood open. Photograph the whole bay in one frame." },
    { id: "wheel", num: 2, n: "Wheels & brakes", enter: "Look at the wheel", d: "Tires, the pressure monitor, and the brakes you can see through the spokes.", fig: "wheel", hint: "Crouch at the front wheel, straight on, so the tire, rim and the brake behind it are all in frame." },

    { id: "under", num: 4, n: "Underside", enter: "Look underneath", d: "Leaks, the exhaust, the suspension and the driveline. A torch and the ground.", fig: "under", hint: "No photo needed yet. The drawing stands in until you have the car raised safely." },
    { id: "body", num: 5, n: "Lights & body", enter: "Walk around", d: "Bulbs, wipers, glass and tint, paint and the small dents.", fig: "body", hint: "A straight side-on photo of the whole car, and one of the rear." }
  ];

        { tier: "S", t: "Service it", d: "Topping up correctly, and getting the oil change on record so the next due date is real instead of guessed.", steps: [{ diy: "j-oilcheck" }, { record: "oil", t: "Log an oil and filter change", why: "A receipt or your own record. /* The path: the one line through everything, Kyle's choice (2026-10-15): strict, in the order a beginner learns a car,
   starting with this car. Only the current step is open; everything after it is locked until the step before is done.
   Order: safety; what the car is telling you and its history; looking and checking, one system at a time, each system
   ending with its G1 study and its Owner quiz; then servicing; then diagnosing; then upgrades; then the Technician
   quizzes and the mock G1.
   Stage kinds:
     ch:   "1.1.1"            a manual chapter (data/manual.js); done when the chapter closes
     g1:   "D1-D10"           G1 study entries (data/g1tasks.js, g1entries.js); done when every task in the range is studied
     quiz: "sus", rung: 1     an area quiz on the certification track; done when passed
     mock: true               the mock G1; done when passed
   park: text  the stage needs a shop, a purchase or a dealer, so it may be set aside; the path moves on and the stage
               stays on the list until its evidence comes in. Nothing else can be skipped.
   tests/path.js checks: every chapter once, every G1 task once, each Owner quiz after its area's Know and Check chapters,
   each Technician quiz after every chapter of its area. */
window.V60_PATH_DATA = [
